comparison: Perfect agreement on salt-dependent nucleosome interactions (C4, C21-C28, C57-C61, C90-C91, C96). Both evaluations support the findings with OpenEval emphasizing Manning theory consistency and peer reviewers highlighting the strength of explicit counterion representation.

Strong agreement on reconciliation of experimental discrepancies (C29-C34, C44-C45, C83, C95). Both evaluations support the mechanistic explanation through restrained vs. unrestrained simulations. Peer reviewers explicitly state the method 'resolves certain experimental discrepancies.'

Strong agreement on computational methodology (C15, C63, C65, C82). Both evaluations support the model design. OpenEval describes it as straightforward methodology while peer reviewers emphasize efficient conformational sampling at low computational cost.

Agreement on model validation (C2, C3, C16, C17, C93, C94). Both support validation through experimental comparison. However, peer evaluation R10 expresses uncertainty about the correlation strength (C84, C85), while OpenEval R1 includes these claims as supported with acknowledgment of moderate correlation.

Divergent evaluations on orientation-distance coupling (C36, C86, C87). OpenEval finds clear support from 2D free energy landscapes, while peer reviewers express uncertainty, noting 'shortage of substantial agreement' in related Figure S4 data.

Agreement on linker histone and NRL effects (C7, C41-C42, C47, C88-C89). Both evaluations support these findings. Peer R4 also includes C6 and C40 (NRL effects without H1), showing broader grouping of linker-dependent phenomena.

Agreement on ion binding dynamics during DNA unwrapping (C18-C20, C43, C92). Both support these findings. Peer reviewers emphasize the strength of explicit counterion representation as a key methodological advantage.

Agreement on sequence-dependent effects (C37-C39). Both evaluations support these findings. OpenEval provides more detailed mechanistic explanation through DNA mechanical properties, while peer reviewers accept implicitly through general validation statements.

Agreement on main biological conclusions (C49, C81). Both support the role of physicochemical interactions in chromatin organization. OpenEval includes additional claims (C46, C48) about pulling experiments and histone modifications that peer reviewers do not explicitly address.

Partial overlap on correlation coefficient claims (C84, C85). OpenEval R1 supports these as part of broader validation, while peer R10 expresses uncertainty about the strength of quantitative agreement, noting moderate correlation may not demonstrate substantial agreement.

Minimal overlap on C5 (orientation-distance coupling energy prediction). OpenEval groups C5 with orientation claims (R5), while peer reviewers group it with experimental discrepancy reconciliation (R3), both supporting the claim but in different contexts.
Minimal overlap on NRL effects (C6, C40). OpenEval R6 addresses sequence and NRL effects together, while peer R4 groups NRL with linker histone effects. Both evaluations support these claims.

OpenEval evaluates reconciliation of simulation predictions with in vivo observations (C50-C54, C97) as UNCERTAIN due to reliance on prior work and speculation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims.

OpenEval evaluates literature context claims (C1, C13-C14, C75) as SUPPORTED, confirming accurate summarization of prior experimental work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.

OpenEval evaluates extensive literature context claims (C8-C12, C72-C74, C76-C80) as SUPPORTED, confirming accurate characterization of established knowledge. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.

OpenEval evaluates methodological justification claims (C62, C66-C71) as SUPPORTED, affirming rationale for model development. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these methodological context claims.
